t.5.51.2: Rightly indeed have you spoken: the killing of an envoy is condemned. But some punishment other than death must certainly be inflicted on him.
t.5.51.1: Having heard those words of his brother, the mighty Daśagrīva spoke in reply words suited to the place and time.
t.5.51.3: The tail, they say, is the cherished ornament of monkeys; let his be set ablaze at once, and let him go with it burnt.
t.5.51.4: Then let all his kinsmen, together with his friends, and his relatives along with his well-wishers, behold this wretched one, emaciated and disfigured in his limbs.
t.5.51.5: The lord of the rākṣasas commanded: "Let him, with his tail ablaze, be led by the rākṣasas around the whole city with its squares."
t.5.51.6: Hearing those words of his, the rākṣasas, harsh with anger, wrapped his tail in worn-out cotton cloths.
t.5.51.7: As his tail was being wrapped all around, the great monkey grew larger, like a fire in the forests that has found dry fuel.
t.5.51.8: Then, having drenched it with oil, they set fire to it there.
t.5.51.9: With his blazing tail he struck down those rākṣasas, his whole being seized by fury and indignation, his face like the rising sun.
t.5.51.10: Bound once more by the cruel rākṣasas who had gathered around him, that heroic best of monkeys formed a resolve suited to the moment.
t.5.51.11: Indeed, even though I am bound, these Rākṣasas are no match for me; breaking the bonds and leaping up, I could slay them once again at will.
t.5.51.12: In battle I am a match for all the rākṣasas; yet for the sake of pleasing Rāma I shall endure even such treatment as this.
t.5.51.14: Let the rākṣasas freely torment me further with bonds and by setting my tail ablaze; my mind feels no weariness at all.
t.5.51.13: "Laṅkā should be roamed through by me once again; that would be well. For by night I did not see it clearly, owing to the arrangement of its fortifications. Laṅkā must surely be seen by me at the close of night."
t.5.51.15: Then the delighted rākṣasas seized the great monkey, that elephant among monkeys, full of courage and with his intentions concealed, and went off with him.
t.5.51.16: With those blasts of conches and kettledrums, the rākṣasas of cruel deeds, proclaiming him by his own deeds, paraded him through that city.
t.5.51.17: Hanumān ranged through the great city of the Rākṣasas, and then the great monkey beheld many wondrous palaces.
t.5.51.18: The monkey surveyed the enclosed tracts of ground, the well-laid-out courtyards, the streets crowded with houses, and the crossroads.
t.5.51.19: In the courtyards, at the crossroads, and likewise along the royal highway, all the rākṣasas proclaimed the monkey, crying, "He is a spy!"
t.5.51.20: Then, as the tip of Hanumān's tail was blazing, those hideous-eyed rākṣasīs reported that unwelcome news to the queen.
t.5.51.21: O Sītā, that copper-faced monkey with whom you held conversation is now being led about with his tail ablaze.
t.5.51.22: Having heard those cruel words, which were like her own abduction all over again, Vaidehī, scorched with grief, approached the fire-god Hutāśana.
t.5.51.23: Then she became intent on the welfare of that great monkey; the large-eyed one, purified and self-restrained, worshipped Agni, the bearer of oblations.
t.5.51.24: If I have truly served my husband, if I have practiced austerity, and if I have been faithful to one husband alone, then be cool to Hanumān.
t.5.51.25: If that wise one has any compassion for me, or if any remnant of good fortune is still mine, then be cool for Hanumān.
t.5.51.26: If that righteous-souled one knows me to be endowed with virtuous conduct and longing for union with him, then be cool for Hanumān.
t.5.51.27: If the noble, mighty-armed Sugrīva, true to his promise, is to deliver me from this sorrow, then be cool for Hanumān.
t.5.51.29: And while his tail was burning, the monkey thought: "Why does this blazing fire not burn me on every side?"
t.5.51.28: Then the fire, sharp-flamed and steady, its flames turning to the right, blazed up as if announcing to the fawn-eyed lady the well-being of the monkey.
t.5.51.30: A great blaze is seen, yet it causes me no pain; resting on the tip of my tail, it is like a fall of cold.
t.5.51.31: Or rather, this is clear: the marvel I saw while leaping, a mountain in the lord of rivers, came about through the power of Rāma.
t.5.51.33: By the compassion of Sītā, by the splendour of Rāghava, and by the friendship of my father, the fire does not burn me.
t.5.51.32: If even the ocean and the wise Maināka showed such zeal for Rāma's sake, what will Agni not do?
t.5.51.34: Once more that elephant among monkeys reflected for a moment; then the great monkey leapt up with force and roared.
t.5.51.35: Then the glorious son of the Wind reached the city gate, lofty like a mountain peak and thronged with rākṣasas posted in separate ranks.
t.5.51.36: Having become like a mountain, he, self-possessed, in an instant again assumed the smallest size and shook off his bonds.
t.5.51.38: Seizing that weapon adorned with black iron, the mighty-armed Māruti once again slew all those guards.
t.5.51.37: Freed, the glorious one became once more like a mountain, and, looking about, he saw an iron bar resting against the gateway.
t.5.51.39: Having slain them, he, fierce in his valor in battle, gazed once more upon Laṅkā, and, wreathed in a garland of flames made by his blazing tail, he shone like the sun garlanded with rays.
